extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (and legislators interested in moral/legal responsibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for what counts as moral virtue, how virtues relate to feelings/actions/capacities, the structure of virtues as means between extremes, and definitions/distinctions for voluntary/involuntary action and moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues are States, not Feelings or Capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are neither Feelings nor Capacities; they are States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feelings (like anger or fear) are experienced without moral choice and are described as being moved; Capacities are natural abilities we possess irrespective of moral quality. Virtues, by contrast, are dispositions or states that involve moral choice and disposition rather than mere feeling or mere ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence produces good condition and good functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: All excellence makes that whereof it is the excellence both to be itself in a good state and to perform its work well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the excellence of the eye makes the eye see well; the excellence of the horse makes it good in speed and in carrying its rider. By analogy, human excellence (virtue) makes a man good and able to perform his proper work well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is a mean state between excess and defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is a middle state between two faulty states, one of excess and the other of defect; it is a mean state apt to exercise deliberate choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean is determined by reason and as the man of practical wisdom would determine. Excess and defect belong to vice; the mean is praiseworthy. This holds for feelings and actions where excess/defect can be identified (e.g., fear, confidence, lust, anger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between absolute mean and relative mean
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an absolute (arithmetical) mean equidistant from extremes and a mean relatively to ourselves which is neither too much nor too little for the particular individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relative mean varies between persons (e.g., what is appropriate nourishment or exercise differs for Milo vs. a novice). Moral virtue aims at the relative mean appropriate to the individual and circumstances rather than a single universal quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some actions/traits are intrinsically bad and admit no mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain actions or qualities (e.g., malevolence, shamelessness, envy, adultery, theft, homicide) are bad in themselves and cannot be made right by reference to a mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such actions are always wrong; the right or wrong does not depend on person/time/manner. You cannot have for them a mean, excess, or defect that is virtuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage as mean regarding fear and confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state in respect of fears and confidence is Courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess = rashness (positive confidence without fear); defect = cowardice (too much fear, too little confidence). Courage aims at feeling fear and confidence to the right extent, toward the right objects, at the right times, for the right reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of Self-Mastery (temperance) as mean regarding pleasures and pains
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state in respect of pleasures and pains (not all pains/pleasures) is perfected Self-Mastery (temperance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect = total absence of self-control; an extreme like insensibility (defect regarding pleasure) is conceivable but rare. The mean appropriately moderates pleasures and pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality regarding giving and taking wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state in giving and taking wealth is Liberality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess = Prodigality (gives too much, takes too little). Defect = Stinginess (takes too much, gives too little). Distinctions to be developed in detail later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Munificence regarding great wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A different mean relating to large-scale wealth is Munificence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Munificence differs from ordinary liberality (concerned with great wealth). Excesses may be called Want of taste or Vulgar Profusion; defect = Paltriness. These extremes differ from those connected with ordinary liberality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of Soul regarding honour and dishonour (large honours)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state with regard to great honour is Greatness of Soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess may be braggadocio; defect = Littleness of Soul. Greatness of Soul aims at appropriate claim to great honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate ambition regarding small honours
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to small honours there is a state analogous to Greatness of Soul but about minor honours; the mean has no single common name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess = Ambitious (grasping at honour more than one should); defect = Unambitious; the virtuous range can sometimes be commended under different names depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meekness as mean regarding anger
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state with respect to anger is Meekness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess = Passionate/Passionateness; defect = Angerlessness/Angerless. Those extremes often lack proper conventional names; the mean is termed Meek or Meekness and is praised when anger is felt at the right time, toward the right persons, for the right reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness regarding speech and disguise of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state in respect of truth is Truthfulness (truthfulness in words/deeds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess (exaggeration) = Braggadocio/Braggadocio; defect (underdrawing) = Reserve/Reserved. The virtuous person speaks truthfully without undue exaggeration or excessive reserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy-pleasantry regarding relaxation and amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state in what is pleasant in relaxation or amusement is Easy-pleasantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess = Buffoonery; defect = Clownishness (insufficient pleasantness). The mean produces agreeable amusement appropriate to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendliness in daily life interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state regarding pleasantness in daily life intercourse is Friendliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess (without interested motive) = Complaisant; with interested motive = Flatterer. Defect = Quarrelsome or Cross. The virtuous mean is being appropriately friendly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shamefacedness as a praised state (moderate shame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shamefacedness (moderate shame) is not a full virtue but is praised as a correct mean in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess = Dumbfoundered (overwhelmed by shame); defect = Shameless. The properly shamefaced person has the appropriate amount of shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indignation as mean between envy and malevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Indignation against successful vice is a state midway between Envy and Malevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rightly-indignant person is annoyed at undeserved success of others; the envious person is annoyed at all success, while the malevolent rejoices at others' misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mean is praiseworthy; degree matters for blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Small deviations from the mean are not blamed; considerable deviations attract blame; moral perception decides borderline cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is difficult to fix exact degrees in words; the Moral Sense judges particulars (what degree of deviation merits blame). Practically one should avoid the extreme more contrary to the mean and sometimes deflect past the wrong side to reach the mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for attaining the mean (practical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To aim at the mean one should guard against the extreme more contrary to the mean and account for one's natural biases (especially bias toward pleasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: remove oneself far from the wrong side and correct back (like straightening bent timber); take the lesser of two evils if exact hitting of the mean is difficult; be particularly wary of pleasure because we judge it partially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of involuntary (compulsion) actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions are compulsory (involuntary) when the origination is external to the agent and the agent contributes nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a wind carrying you, another person having power over you. Mixed cases (e.g., throwing goods overboard in a storm) may be 'of a mixed kind' but are often most like voluntary actions when the agent's origination/motion rests with himself for the reasons of safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of involuntary actions from ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done by reason of ignorance can be involuntary provided they are accompanied by pain and remorse; mere ignorance without regret does not make an action involuntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ignorance of principle (blamable) from ignorance of particular details of the action (which can excuse). The agent who regrets after acting from ignorance is considered involuntary; one who does not regret is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars whose ignorance can render action involuntary
rubrics_metrics.description: The particulars relevant to whether ignorance makes an action involuntary include: who acts, what he is doing, with respect to what or in what, sometimes with what instrument, with what result, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignorance of the agent himself is implausible, but ignorance of what one is doing or of the result can ground involuntariness. The more important the particular (especially those in which the action consists and its result), the more it supports the plea of involuntariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary action defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary action is that whose origination is in the agent, the agent being aware of the particular details in which the action consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions done from anger or lust may still be voluntary; voluntary is the broader class (includes actions not involving moral choice); origination in the agent and awareness of particulars are key. Mixed cases (compulsion, choices made to avoid greater evils) are judged by the agent's origination and present choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice (prohairesis) is distinct from mere voluntary action and from passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is plainly voluntary but not identical with voluntary actions, nor with lust, anger, wish, or opinion; it concerns the choice of means to ends within our power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice requires deliberation and is tied to practical wisdom; it selects means (not impossible ends), forms character by choosing good/bad things, and is commended for having a right object. It is not shared by irrational animals or children and is different from wish (which can aim at impossible ends) and from opinion (true/false rather than good/bad).
